# The nixpkgs FHS sandbox: what kiro can and cannot see

> **Last verified:** 2026-10-14 — the FHS chat wrapper passes trust grants to
> the payload, which resolves ACP engine settings before applying them.
>
> Full lineage: `git show 0057d8ed:packages/kiro-cli/docs/fhs-sandbox.md`.

**This is not Kiro's sandbox.** It is an upstream nixpkgs wrapper: since the
package split, `pkgs.ai.kiro-cli` on Linux routes all three commands through one
shared `buildFHSEnv` sandbox. `$out/bin/*` are thin command-selecting wrappers;
`$out/libexec/kiro-cli/kiro-cli-wrapper` is the bubblewrap launcher.

**It is also a different axis from Kiro's own workspace-root allowlist** (see
`dev/references/kiro-workflow-ref.md`). The discriminator is cheap: bwrap has no
concept of a workspace root and would never mention `additionalDirectories`. An
error naming an allowed root is the other axis; this one produces "command not
found" and loader failures.

**None of it applies to darwin**, where upstream returns
`kiro-cli-unwrapped.overrideAttrs` and builds no FHS layer at all — verified
byte-identical across every unwrapped-era nixpkgs checkout in the store. A Mac
sees no change from this wrapper, Homebrew included.

## The bind rule

```bash
for dir in /*; do
  if [[ -d "$dir" ]] && [[ -z "${ignored_set[$dir]:-}" ]]; then
    auto_mounts+=(--bind "$dir" "$dir")   # read-write, same path
  fi
done
```

`ignored_set` is the rootfs top level — exactly
`bin etc lib lib32 lib64 libexec nix-support sbin usr` — plus a hardcoded
`/nix /dev /proc /etc`. Everything else is bound **read-write** at the same
path: `/home`, `/opt`, `/var`, `/tmp`, `/snap`, `/mnt`, `/srv`, `/root`, all
`rw,nosuid,nodev`.

Three exclusions the loop's shape hides, all measured:

- **Hidden entries are silently dropped.** `/*` does not glob dot-entries, so a
  real `/.config` on the host is simply absent inside.
- **Non-directories are skipped** — `/swapfile` and friends.
- **`-d` follows symlinks**, so a top-level symlink _into_ a shadowed subtree
  re-exposes its target. Host `/libx32 -> usr/libx32` is not in the ignore set,
  so host `/usr/libx32` appears read-write at `/libx32` — a hole in the "`/usr`
  is replaced" story.

`/nix`, `/dev` and `/proc` are not "shadowed" either: `/nix` is bound
read-write, `/dev` is a `--dev-bind`, `/proc` is a fresh procfs in the **host
PID namespace** (no `--unshare-pid`; all six `unshare*` options default false).
Host `/etc` stays readable at `/.host-etc`. Meanwhile `/lib32` inside becomes a
**dangling** symlink to a `/usr/lib32` the rootfs does not provide, even though
the host has the real one.

## PATH survives; the entries on it may not

`/etc/profile` does `export PATH="/run/wrappers/bin:/usr/bin:/usr/sbin:$PATH"`
and nothing passes `--clearenv`, so the inherited PATH is preserved intact
(measured: `~/.nix-profile/bin` survives; `jq` and `treefmt` resolve to their
store paths).

**Preserved is not still-valid, and the failure mode is quiet.** The inherited
PATH still lists `/usr/local/sbin:/usr/local/bin:/usr/sbin:/usr/bin`, all now
dead or pointing elsewhere:

| tool                                            | inside the sandbox               |
| ----------------------------------------------- | -------------------------------- |
| `nrfutil` — only in `/usr/local/bin`            | not resolvable                   |
| `lazygit` — in `/usr/local/bin` AND nix profile | resolves, but to the **nix** one |

The second row is the dangerous one: no error, a different build of the same
tool. A version-sensitive step changes behavior instead of failing.

The same ordering affects Kiro's own dispatch. With no chat-specific
configuration, the synthesized `/usr/bin` contains the raw `kiro-cli-chat`, so a
normal `kiro-cli` launch finds it before the inherited profile PATH reaches any
outer wrapper. When `trustedMcpTools` is non-empty, this repo re-composes
nixpkgs' FHS package around a chat-only wrapped payload instead. The command at
that same `/usr/bin` path is then the configured wrapper, so launcher-dispatched
devenv sessions do not silently lose the grant. It passes the grant through a
private environment value to the payload launcher, which resolves ACP engine
settings before deciding whether `--trust-tools` is accepted and clears that
value before native execution.

## Supplying missing tools

Use `ai.kiro.cli.extraPackages` for tools Kiro needs but the synthesized root
does not provide:

```nix
ai.kiro.cli.extraPackages = with pkgs; [
  file
  iproute2
  tree
  which
];
```

The Kiro launcher prepends `lib.makeBinPath` of those packages to PATH and then
preserves the caller's PATH. If `ai.kiro.cli.environmentVariables.PATH` is set,
that explicit value becomes the preserved base instead. The wrapper references
each package, so its store path is rooted; bubblewrap preserves the resulting
PATH and bind-mounts `/nix`, so the tools remain executable inside the FHS root.
Setting that Kiro-specific PATH entry to null suppresses a root
`ai.environmentVariables.PATH`; the ambient PATH becomes the preserved base.

This supplies commands missing from the synthesized root; it is not an override
mechanism for commands already there. After the outer launcher runs, the FHS
`/init` sources `/etc/profile`, which puts
`/run/wrappers/bin:/usr/bin:/usr/sbin` ahead of the inherited entries. A
same-named FHS command therefore wins over the added package on Linux.

## Opting out of the FHS wrapper

The default stays upstream-compatible:

```nix
ai.kiro.cli.useFhsSandbox = true;
```

Consumers willing to give up the extracted-`bun` compatibility fix can select
the pinned unwrapped payload explicitly:

```nix
ai.kiro.cli.useFhsSandbox = false;
```

That removes bubblewrap from Kiro's launch chain and restores the host's normal
namespace and PATH resolution. It does not select a separately packaged binary:
rollout patches, version pinning, TERM defaults, environment variables, secrets,
build-time KAS selection, and argv injection still use the same overlay payload
and wrapper helpers. A custom `ai.kiro.cli.package` must expose
`passthru.unwrapped` on every rollout-resolved variant; otherwise evaluation
fails with a named assertion instead of silently retaining the sandbox. Direct
package consumers can make the same choice with `pkgs.ai.kiro-cli.unwrapped`.
The overlay exposes that route even on pre-split nixpkgs (reachable only when a
consumer sets `follows` or lands on the overlay's fallback), where it selects
the already-direct package and is therefore a no-op.

With the sandbox enabled, a custom FHS package used with `trustedMcpTools` must
also expose `passthru.withFhsPayload`. Without it the FHS command shadows the
outer chat wrapper and silently drops the grant, so the module rejects that
detectable package shape. A package that is already direct can state that
explicitly with `passthru.kiroFhsSandbox = false`; the overlay does so for
darwin and pre-split nixpkgs.

The cost is real. nixpkgs added the FHS environment because Kiro dynamically
extracts a generic-glibc `bun`; without the compatibility root, that path may
fail on NixOS or another non-FHS host. This is why the option is default-on and
opt-out rather than an automatic platform guess.

`ai.shell` remains `null` by default. The module does not silently choose a
shell merely because the FHS root contains bash and may hide a host zsh. Set
`ai.shell = pkgs.bashInteractive` for a store-backed explicit shell, or opt out
of FHS when preserving host namespace behavior is the intended tradeoff.

`packages/kiro-cli/checks/kiro-fhs-contract.nix` guards the upstream assumptions
behind this behavior. It verifies that all three public command wrappers select
the shared FHS launcher, then inspects that launcher and fails if bubblewrap
stops binding `/nix`, adds a known PATH-clearing or replacement argument,
changes how the generated `/etc` is mounted, moves `/etc/profile` sourcing after
Kiro's exec, changes the shared command dispatcher, adds another
init/profile/dispatcher PATH mutation, or removes the incoming PATH from the
profile assignment. It also builds a `trustedMcpTools` configuration and proves
the synthesized `/usr/bin/kiro-cli-chat` resolves to the trust wrapper. Those
structural changes therefore force this document and the implementation to be
re-measured instead of silently invalidating `extraPackages` or the devenv trust
grant.

The check is deliberately structural. It does not execute bubblewrap inside a
Nix build sandbox, where nested user-namespace support is not portable. The
wrapper sentinel test covers the configured prefix and inherited tail; the FHS
contract check pins the current launcher/init/profile literals and their
ordering. Together they cover the known structural bridge, not kernel-level
execution of it.

This is runtime-local: it changes neither the Home Manager session nor the
devenv project shell. Adding the same packages to `home.packages` or devenv's
`packages` also works when user- or project-wide availability is wanted, since
those store-backed profile entries already survive into Kiro.

Do not model this as arbitrary host paths. Visibility under `/home` or `/opt`
does not guarantee a host-built binary can load its libraries, and host `/usr`
is the directory the FHS wrapper replaces.

## `/usr/local` is unreachable, and the obvious escape hatch hard-fails

The rootfs `/usr` supplies `bin include lib lib64 libexec sbin share` and no
`local`, so `/usr/local` is **absent** inside. `/proc/<pid>/root` does not get
around it: the bwrap child user namespace cannot ptrace parent-userns processes,
so both `/proc/1/root` and a same-user host PID return **Permission denied**.

The builder exposes `extraBwrapArgs` and it IS appended last — but a trailing
`--bind /usr/local /usr/local` is not a fix:

```console
bwrap: Can't mkdir /usr/local: Read-only file system
```

A **hard launch failure**, not a silent no-op, which matters because "last mount
wins" is the natural expectation. The blocker is the `mkdir`, not the ordering:
binding _over_ an entry the rootfs already has works fine (measured —
`--bind /usr/local /usr/include` succeeded). Two shapes that do work:

- **measured** — bind to a destination outside the shadowed subtree, e.g.
  `--bind /usr/local /usr-local`.
- **inferred** — `extraBuildCommands` to `mkdir -p $out/usr/local` in the
  rootfs, then the trailing bind, since the mountpoint would then exist.

`extraBindMounts` does not exist in this builder. Do not cite it.

## Visibility is necessary, not sufficient

This is where the sandbox actually bites, and it is not a path problem.

- The FHS `/usr/bin` holds **exactly 233 entries** — coreutils, shadow, glibc,
  gawk, gnused, gnugrep, gnutar, diffutils, findutils, less, the compressors,
  wl-clipboard, and the three `kiro-cli*` binaries. There is **no `node`, no
  `python3`, no `perl`.**
- A repo-local `node_modules/.bin/<tool>` **does** run — measured,
  `pnpm --version` → `10.27.0` — but only because its `#!/usr/bin/env node`
  found node in the user's nix profile. The same tree with an apt-installed
  `/usr/bin/node` fails, because that interpreter is shadowed.
- **A host-built dynamically-linked binary can be visible and still not run.**
  Measured: `/opt/nodejs/node-v18.4.0-linux-x64/bin/node` fails with
  `libstdc++.so.6: cannot open shared object file` — even though that library is
  present at `/usr/lib64`. Root cause: `/etc/ld.so.conf` and `/etc/ld.so.cache`
  do not exist inside. The launcher symlinks glibc's copies _at_ those paths but
  nothing ever creates them, so the loader never searches `/usr/lib64`.
  `LD_LIBRARY_PATH=/usr/lib64` makes the same binary run.

So for anything outside the nix store, assume it needs its libraries found for
it. **Homebrew was not measurable** on the probe host (no `/home/linuxbrew`,
`/opt/homebrew`, or `/usr/local/Homebrew` present), so on Linux treat "linuxbrew
binaries work" as UNVERIFIED: the `/home` and `/opt` binds assure visibility,
nothing here assures execution. On darwin the question does not arise — there is
no sandbox.

## Diagnostic

```bash
# Does the package expose the shared bwrap path? Then these rules apply.
K=$(nix build --no-link --print-out-paths .#ciPackages.x86_64-linux.kiro-cli)
readlink -f "$K/libexec/kiro-cli/kiro-cli-wrapper"
ls /nix/store/*-kiro-cli-*fhsenv-rootfs/usr/bin | wc -l   # 233 = the whole world
```

## Kiro launch defaults and argument composition

> **Last verified:** 2026-10-14 — ACP reads engine settings in the payload
> launchers; the packaged KAS wins over inherited overrides.
>
> Full historical measurements:
> `git show 8be06935:packages/kiro-cli/docs/launcher-argv.md`. KAS file-backed
> prompts persist per conversation and inherit through workflow children and
> forks.

### Terminal and ACP have different consumers

Managed library, Home Manager and devenv configurations default
`cli.native.settings.chat.agentEngine` to `"v3"` through the existing settings
writer. Native terminal selection is explicit CLI > repository settings > global
settings. There is no terminal `--v3` injection. Every module feature is built
and tested against V3; other native engine values, including null (automatic
selection), warn. V3-only features additionally reject incompatible
declarations.

ACP does not read persisted `chat.agentEngine` itself. The payload's existing
`makeWrapper` launchers read `$KIRO_HOME/settings/cli.json` (default
`~/.kiro/settings/cli.json`) then `./.kiro/settings/cli.json`, with the repo
value winning. On `acp` only, they add `--agent-engine <value>` when a value
exists and no explicit engine flag was supplied. Both `--agent-engine` spellings
and launcher `--v1`, `--v2`, `--v3` win. Shared argv helpers skip value-taking
globals when recognizing ACP and stop at `--`. Without a setting, argv stays
unchanged. Settings changes do not create a new payload derivation.

Devenv's `.kiro` output, including the engine setting, applies when starting
Kiro at the project root: Kiro does not find that root from a subdirectory.

### Package and platform composition

`withBundlePatches` and `withRolloutFeatures` preserve each other. Linux applies
the settings bridge in the unwrapped payload before nixpkgs builds the FHS root
around it. `useFhsSandbox = false` selects that same payload directly.

Darwin's launcher shim executes the real packaged `.app` binary and sets argv0
to that path; an app-shaped argv0 alone on a hidden `bin` symlink was
insufficient in native CI. The native launcher discovers the app's chat binary
directly. Consequently the main launcher also supplies the ACP default, while
direct `bin/kiro-cli-chat` has its own guarded default. Never change the Darwin
shim to `exec -a "$0"`: it must retain the real app path as executable and
argv0.

The packaged KAS always wins: both launchers set `KIRO_KAS_SERVER_PATH` with
`--set`. A differing inherited path produces one stderr line saying it was
detected and ignored and naming the selected path; the same path is silent. The
main launcher exports the selected path before dispatch, so the direct chat
launcher does not repeat the warning. TERM and platform setup remain ordinary
build wrapper arguments. No wrapper injects `--tui`.

### Trust injection remains engine-sensitive

`--trust-tools` is a chat-subcommand option, so the payload launcher adds it to
`chat` and `acp` only. ACP with V3 rejects it, while terminal V3 accepts it. The
payload first resolves the effective ACP engine from argv and settings, then
applies the configured trust grant only when that engine accepts it. The
module's chat wrapper hands the grant through `NAT_KIRO_TRUST_TOOLS`; the
payload unsets that private value before executing the native binary. This order
prevents a repository V3 override from receiving a conflicting `--trust-tools`
flag.

Linux's FHS root supplies `/usr/bin/kiro-cli-chat` ahead of inherited PATH. An
outer chat wrapper would be bypassed on launcher dispatch, so trust handling is
placed in the selected payload with `withFhsPayload`. Environment exports and
extra packages remain outside, inherited through bubblewrap. Custom packages
advertising an FHS payload must support this recomposition or evaluation refuses
the configuration.

Home Manager also translates representable `trustedMcpTools` entries into
`permissions.yaml` when the effective declared engine is V3. Devenv does not
have this permissions writer; withholding the ACP flag there does not create an
equivalent declarative grant. The external ACP client owns interactive approval.

Do not infer feature availability from KAS/TUI JavaScript alone: the Rust chat
binary recomputes the enabled rollout list before spawning the frontend.
Friendly features and global-only client settings are documented in
[workflow-gating.md](workflow-gating.md).

### Verification

- `checks/native-startup.py` runs both native entry points with no prompt and
  checks the launch decision before input validation. Opposing global/repository
  values and explicit flags prove engine selection, not just settings reads.
- `checks/kas-dispatch.py` captures the selected KAS under fresh and stale
  homes, checks default ACP and both explicit V2 spellings on main/direct entry
  points, and initializes real ACP without a model turn.
- `checks/kiro-wrapper-argv.nix` exercises remaining trust, environment and PATH
  handling against dispatching stubs.
- `checks/kiro-fhs-contract.nix` checks the selected rootfs payload and
  inherited PATH bridge. Nested bubblewrap execution is a separate host test
  because Nix build sandboxes cannot reliably create nested user namespaces.

The module wrapper still ends in `exec -a "$0" <realBin> "$@"`; the behavioral
check reads that shape. This contract is separate from the Darwin build shim's
app-path argv0 requirement.

### File-backed prompts and conversation snapshots

KAS reads the flat `chat.promptFiles` object from global and repository
`settings/cli.json` at conversation creation. The semantic slots are `identity`,
`workflowFileCheckGuidance` and `worktreeGuidance`. It starts with the three
selected packaged texts, overlays global slots, then repository slots. Existing
identity selection determines that slot's default, preserving its on/off
behavior. Enabled worktree policy customizes the selected worktree guidance with
the admitted sibling root while preserving workflow-owned creation and requiring
user-controlled PR merging. The blanket steering-strip tweak is retired. The
file-check slot retains the vendor absolute-path text; sibling roots use
`chat.additionalDirectories` rather than the retired relative-path workaround. A
null slot restores the packaged selection. The global root is `KIRO_HOME` when
set, otherwise the session home plus `.kiro`; relative global paths use the
settings file directory, while repository paths use the session working
directory. Regular UTF-8 files up to 1 MiB are accepted, including empty text.
Malformed settings, files or persisted snapshots fail visibly.

The session owns a frozen resolved snapshot. Initial metadata persistence must
succeed before creation returns; `_meta.kiro.nixPromptSnapshot` is reserved and
client metadata cannot supply or replace it. Resident and cold resumes retain
the original slots even after files change or disappear. The per-session
registry applies the workflow creator slot when bundled profiles register or
refresh. Existing custom-agent precedence and permission objects are preserved.
Internal workflow children inherit through the trusted owner-session carrier,
including persisted owners. Forks copy the validated snapshot with their
selected metadata. No process-global current prompt exists.

Identity remains inside the vendor renderers and retains their template
semantics. Worktree guidance is appended directly to the workflow instructions;
the bundled workflow creator has no template pass. File text is not a new
plain-text rendering language: `{{worktree_path}}` resolves only at the existing
workflow input boundary. JavaScript-looking text is data, not executable code.
Dynamic environment, workspace, date, steering and tool context still come from
the vendor constructors.

Legacy saved conversations lack historical auxiliary slots. They keep their
persisted initial message and use the packaged auxiliary defaults rather than
reading current override files; historical auxiliary text cannot be recovered.
Explicit V2 dispatch bypasses KAS entirely, so manually written prompt-file
settings cannot enforce a runtime V2 conflict error. This feature adds no
configuration-reading wrapper or native-binary patch.

`checks/prompt-files.mjs` extracts actual patched constructors, lifecycle and
registry methods into an isolated VM with inert host services. It captures the
Vibe/custom initial messages and both request representations (`systemPrompt`
and first message), plus concurrent session creation, strict save failure,
resident/cold resume, owner inheritance and registry refresh. It does not invoke
a model or authenticate. The transport adapter stops before vendor history
conversion and network I/O; separate package dispatch smoke covers startup.

### Prompt corpus and the static/runtime boundary

Build `ciPackages.<system>.kiro-cli.kas.promptCorpus` explicitly to inspect the
original release server. This is the `corpus` output of the same selected KAS
derivation, generated before any text changes or hooks. Its ranges and source
hash describe those original bytes, not the installed patched server. The
runtime `out` does not reference it, and both proprietary outputs retain the
`kiro-cli` cache exclusion prefix. After selected text changes, a temporary
second extraction supplies matching ranges and a checked hash to the lifecycle
patcher. Core slot placement follows those semantic corpus entries; lifecycle
methods use unique AST shapes and refuse changed anchors. There is no installed
stock KAS dependency or evaluation-time extraction.

`extract/prompts.mjs` uses the existing TypeScript parser. It reads every string
literal and every template's static chunks, including short strings, with UTF-8
byte ranges into the fingerprinted source. Untagged chunks contain cooked text.
Chunks marked `tagged: true` contain TypeScript parser text, not a promised
cooked or effective value: legal invalid escapes in tagged templates can have an
undefined cooked value. It does not import KAS or evaluate vendor expressions.
Isolated evaluation cannot recover session-dependent prompt builders without
fabricating runtime services, so AST extraction is the narrower technique here.
The entire literal index is a searchable superset, **not a claim that every
bundled string is a prompt**.

Five inspected entry points are named separately: identity, system features,
Vibe, workflow creator and workflow orchestration. Each points to its decoded
chunk and containing callable's range when one exists. Select their source
ranges in the matching original release source to inspect callers and branches;
minified names are not stable identifiers. The corpus also contains the
workspace, shell, steering, tool-description, spec, agent-profile and memory
guidance those entry points alone do not enumerate. No keyword or length filter
excludes newly shipped strings.

Each JavaScript template records an ordered sequence of chunk references and
exact interpolation expressions with source ranges, with tagged chunks subject
to the parser-text limitation above. Nested templates have their own records.
Expressions such as clock reads, workspace lookups, feature branches and helper
calls remain unevaluated. Mustache-shaped text such as `{{machineId}}` and
`{{worktree_path}}` remains decoded literal text: it is a later formatting
boundary, not JavaScript interpolation. Concatenation, conditional inclusion,
session state, external prompt files, and saved-session prompt reuse remain
runtime assembly; the corpus does not claim to reconstruct the effective prompt
of a session. In particular, a persisted initial system message may bypass fresh
prompt construction.

`lib/kiro-bundle-patch.py` finds the existing named selections in these decoded
chunks, checks the source fingerprint and uniqueness, and replaces only the
selected token contents. Quoting changes in a release no longer invalidate a
decoded match. Serialization escapes the actual quote and template delimiters,
preserving interpolation expressions. Tagged templates are refused because a tag
may interpret raw escapes differently. Missing or duplicate decoded matches fail
closed before any output write.

The existing owner extraction/check/regeneration contract carries the corpus
digest, chunk/template counts and named groups alongside other Kiro facts. These
measurements remain raw drift evidence, not an unused declared API. The real
vendor check consumes named groups to assert the inspected entry points and
their interpolation boundaries. Full vendor prompt text stays in the explicit
inspection artifact, not the committed fact files. Ordinary module/package
evaluation reads committed facts and never realizes this corpus through IFD.

Inspect the full corpus with Node or Python: JavaScript strings can contain lone
UTF-16 surrogate code units, which the JSON preserves but `jq` rejects. The
facts pipeline reads only the scalar summary through Node before combining it
with other facts.

The extraction sources stay distinct:

| Artifact                      | Facts                                     | Technique                                                                              |
| ----------------------------- | ----------------------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| KAS JavaScript                | Hook vocabulary, prompt corpus            | Static TypeScript AST; decoded literal text and unresolved expressions                 |
| Native chat executable        | Rollout manifest and patchability         | Validated text matching against embedded manifest entries                              |
| Public documentation snapshot | Model suggestions                         | Separate `kiro-model-catalog` owner and document parser                                |
| TUI JavaScript                | Settings registry and workspace allowlist | Sandboxed host materialization, then AST validation and isolated expression evaluation |

`kiro-bundle-patch` executes synthetic fixtures across single, double and
template quotes, UTF-8 offsets, escaped content and runtime holes; it refuses
stale corpora, tagged selections and anchor drift. The real
`kiro-bundle-patch-drift` check runs on both native builders, compares both
identity selections, checks JavaScript syntax, executes only the changed
standalone literal tokens to verify their values, and proves all other decoded
text and source bytes survive. Existing KAS resource, initialization and
dispatch checks remain in place. Native Darwin execution is CI evidence; parsing
a Darwin bundle on Linux alone is not that evidence.
